subject: Cognitive Science
title: Learning from Patterns
description: A 60-second lesson on Learning from Patterns.

hook.text: Every swan you've ever seen is white. You conclude all swans are white. Then you visit Australia.

buildup.text: Inductive reasoning draws general conclusions from specific observations. It's powerful but never certain.

discovery.text: Unlike deduction, induction gives probable conclusions, not guaranteed ones. More data raises confidence.

twist.text: One black swan destroys the rule. Induction is always vulnerable to the next observation.

climax.text: All of science runs on induction: observe, find patterns, test. It works—until it doesn't.

quiz.question: What is the key weakness of inductive reasoning?

details.summary: Inductive reasoning generalizes from specific observations to broader principles. Seeing many white swans leads to the conclusion that all swans are white. Induction is how we build knowledge from experience, but it can never provide certainty because the next observation might be a black swan.
details.whyItMatters: Almost all empirical knowledge is inductive. Understanding its strengths and limits is essential for evaluating scientific claims and everyday generalizations.
takeaways: Induction moves from specific observations to general principles
It provides probable conclusions, never certain ones
More diverse confirming evidence strengthens inductive conclusions

faq.question: What is the problem of induction?
faq.answer: David Hume argued that no amount of past observations logically guarantees future observations. The sun has risen every day, but nothing in logic ensures it will rise tomorrow. We rely on induction because it works, but we cannot prove that it will continue to work.

faq.question: How can you make inductive reasoning stronger?
faq.answer: Increase the number and diversity of observations. Look for confirming evidence in varied contexts, not just the same one. Actively seek disconfirming cases. The more varied the evidence supporting a generalization, the stronger the induction.
